exercises.name: Forearm Roll
exercises.note: Tennis elbow almost never starts at the elbow. It starts in the forearm muscles that grip the racket and brake the wrist on every shot, and the elbow is just where they attach and complain. Five minutes a week on the forearm itself is worth more than any brace you can buy.

good: Forearm across the roller on a table or the floor, roll slowly from elbow to wrist
Do the top of the forearm first. That is the side that gives you tennis elbow
Stop on a sore spot and slowly open and close your fist a few times
bad: Rolling straight over the bony point of the elbow

good: Arm straight out, palm down, gently bend the wrist so the fingers point at the floor
Pull with the other hand, softly. You should feel the top of the forearm
bad: Bending the elbow to make it easier
Pulling hard. This one is easy to overdo and it bites back

good: Arm straight out, palm up, gently bend the wrist so the fingers point at the floor
Now you should feel the underside of the forearm

exercises.name: Lat Roll
exercises.note: The lat is the biggest muscle in your serve and the one that goes quietly tight. It is also the reason a stiff shoulder sometimes will not free up no matter how much you stretch the shoulder itself. Your serving side will be the worse one. Give it the extra time.

good: On your side, arm overhead, roller under the armpit and down the side of the back
Small movements. Pause where it bites and breathe
Roller across the upper back, hands behind the head, ribs down
Pause and breathe at each level before moving up
Stay above the bottom of the ribcage. The lower back does not get rolled
bad: Arching over the roller and letting the ribs flare

good: Arm straight across the chest, pull it in with the other forearm
Shoulder stays down, not shrugged towards the ear
bad: Pushing into a pinch at the front of the shoulder. Back off if you feel one

good: Forearm on the door frame, elbow at shoulder height, step through and turn away
bad: Letting the shoulder roll forward into it
